'''Charles Alderson Janeway, Jr.''' (February 5, 1943 &ndash; April 12, 2003) was an American [[immunologist]] who helped create the modern field of [[innate immunity]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/04/27/nyregion/dr-charles-janeway-jr-60-expert-on-immune-system-dies.html|title=Dr. Charles Janeway Jr., 60, Expert on Immune System, Dies|last=O'Connor|first=Anahad|date=2003-04-27|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-25|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> A member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]], he held a faculty position at [[Yale University]]'s Medical School and was an [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] Investigator.

== Early life and education ==
Born in [[Boston]] on February 5, 1943, to Charles A. and Elizabeth B. Janeway, Charles Janeway was raised in [[Weston, Massachusetts]]. He was educated at [[Phillips Exeter Academy]] in New Hampshire, and [[Harvard College]], where he graduated ''summa cum laude'' in 1963 with a bachelor's degree in chemistry. His interest in medicine was inspired by his parents: his father [[Charles Alderson Janeway]] was physician-in-chief at Boston Children's Hospital from 1946 to 1974 and his mother was a social worker at the [[Brigham and Women's Hospital|Boston Lying-In Hospital]].

By earning his medical degree from [[Harvard Medical School]] in 1969, Janeway joined a long family line of prominent physicians. In addition to his father, his grandfather, [[Theodore C. Janeway]], was the first full-time professor of medicine at the [[Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine]], and his great-grandfather, [[Edward Gamaliel Janeway|Edward G. Janeway]], was the [[Commissioner of Health of the City of New York]].

== Career ==
Janeway trained in basic-science research with [[Hugh McDevitt]] at Harvard, [[John H. Humphrey|John Humphrey]] at the National Institute for Medical Research in England, and with [[Robin Coombs]] at [[Cambridge University]] in England. He completed an [[internal medicine]] internship at the Peter Bent Brigham Hospital in Boston.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Janeway|first=Charles A.|date=2002|title=A Trip Through my Life With an Immunological Theme|journal=Annual Review of Immunology|language=en|volume=20|issue=1|pages=1–28|doi=10.1146/annurev.immunol.20.080801.102422|pmid=11861595|issn=0732-0582|doi-access=free}}</ref> Following five years of immunology research at the [[National Institutes of Health]] in Bethesda, Md., under [[William E. Paul]], and two years at [[Uppsala University]] in Sweden under Hans Wigzell, he joined the faculty of Yale University in 1977. In 1983, he was promoted to Professor of Pathology. In 1998, he was a founding member of the Section of Immunobiology at [[Yale University School of Medicine]].

Janeway was one of the leading immunologists of his generation, studying the [[innate immune system]] and the biology of [[T cell]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Medzhitov|first=R.|date=2013-11-01|title=Pattern Recognition Theory and the Launch of Modern Innate Immunity|journal=The Journal of Immunology|language=en|volume=191|issue=9|pages=4473–4474|doi=10.4049/jimmunol.1302427|issn=0022-1767|pmid=24141853|doi-access=free}}</ref> In 1989, he predicted that activation of the adaptive immune response is controlled by the more ancient innate immune system recognizing patterns of pathogens.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Medzhitov|first=Ruslan|title=Approaching the Asymptote: 20 Years Later|journal=Immunity|year=2009|volume=30|issue=6|pages=766–775|doi=10.1016/j.immuni.2009.06.004|pmid=19538928|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Janeway made fundamental contributions to many other areas of immunology, including co-discovery of bacterial [[superantigen]]s.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Janeway Jr.|first=Charles|title=An external stimulus that mimics Mls locus responses|journal=European Journal of Immunogenetics|year=1988|volume=15|issue=1–3|pages=161–168|doi=10.1111/j.1744-313X.1988.tb00418.x|pmid=3148661|s2cid=30526749|display-authors=etal}}</ref> Together with [[Alexander Rudensky]], Janeway also characterized how self antigens associate with [[MHC class II]] molecules.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Rudensky|first=Alexander |author2=Preston-Hurlburt P |author3=Hong SC |author4=Barlow A |author5=Janeway CA Jr|title=Sequence analysis of peptides bound to MHC class II molecules|journal=Nature|year=1991|volume=353|pages=622–627|pmid=1656276 | doi = 10.1038/353622a0 |issue = 6345|bibcode=1991Natur.353..622R |s2cid=4341627 }}</ref>

Janeway is particularly well known as the lead author of ''Immunobiology'', a standard textbook on [[immunology]]. Since the 2008 publishing of its seventh edition, it has been renamed as ''Janeway's Immunobiology'' in his memory.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gulati |first=Poonam |date=March 2009 |title=Janeway's Immunobiology, 7th Edition by Kenneth Murphy, Paul Travers, and Mark Walport |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/bmb.20272 |journal=Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Education |language=en |volume=37 |issue=2 |pages=134 |doi=10.1002/bmb.20272|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He also published more than 300 scientific papers.

Janeway also served on the board of directors of several research institutes, including the [[Trudeau Institute]], and the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology. He was president of the [[American Association of Immunologists]] from 1997 to 1998.

Janeway was married to [[H. Kim Bottomly]], Ph.D., and had three daughters: Katherine A. Janeway, M.D., Hannah H. Janeway, M.D., and Megan G. Janeway, M.D. He died of [[B-cell lymphoma]] on April 12, 2003, in his home in [[New Haven, Connecticut]].<ref name=":0" />

== Awards ==

* 1991 Bohmfalk Teaching Award, Yale University
* 2001 [[American Association of Immunologists Lifetime Achievement Award]]<ref name="Winners">{{cite web |title=Past Recipients |url=https://www.aai.org/Awards/Career-Awards/AAI-Lifetime-Achievement-Award/Past-Recipients.aspx |access-date=19 September 2018 |website=The American Association of Immunologists}}</ref>
* 2002 German Society for Immunology Avery-Landsteiner Award
* 2003 [[Cancer Research Institute]] [[William B. Coley Award]]
